 Medicare’s 2027 Part B Premium Takes $6.50 of Your 3.6% Social Security COLA
 Maurie Backman Fri, November 20, 2026 at 1:39 AM PST 4 min read Quick Read 
 Medicare Part B premiums rise $6.50 to $209.40 monthly in 2027, a far smaller jump than 2026's $17.90 increase, trimming the 3.6% COLA. 
 The average retiree collecting $2,095 monthly gains about $75 from the COLA, but keeps roughly $69 after the Part B hike, or $822 yearly. 
 Higher earners above $112,000 individually or $224,000 jointly face IRMAA surcharges, while all seniors can lower costs by switching plans before Dec. 7 open enrollment ends.

 When the Social Security Administration announced in mid-October that benefits would receive a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) for 2027, many seniors were happy with the news. In 2026, Social Security benefits only rose 2.8%, so a 3.6% increase is far more generous. 
 Canva | izusek from Getty Images Signature and DNY59 from Getty Images Signature But for weeks, there was still a piece of the puzzle left to unravel: How much would Medicare Part B increase for 2027? 
 That's an important question to ask because seniors enrolled in Social Security and Medicare pay for Part B, which covers outpatient care, out of their monthly benefits automatically. Whenever the cost of Part B premiums increases from one year to the next, it's effectively deducted from seniors' COLAs, leaving them with smaller raises. 
 Now that we know how much Part B premiums are set to increase in 2027, seniors can calculate exactly how much extra money their upcoming COLA will give them. 
 Medicare Part B will cost $6.50 more per month in 2027 
 It's common for the cost of Part B to increase from one year to the next. In 2026, the cost of Part B rose by $17.90 compared to 2025. Thankfully, the 2027 increase is more modest, coming in at just $6.50.

 The current standard Medicare Part B premium is $202.90 per month. In 2027, it will be $209.40. Some Social Security recipients, however, could pay a lot more for Part B if they're subject to surcharges known as income-related monthly adjustment amounts (IRMAAs). 
 Story Continues The good news is that seniors whose income is high enough to warrant IRMAAs may not have to worry about losing a portion of their Social Security COLA to higher Medicare costs. In 2027, IRMAAs begin to apply to seniors with an individual income above $112,000 or joint filers with an income above $224,000. 
 Calculating your actual 2027 raise 
 Now that you know how much Social Security benefits are rising in the new year and what Medicare will cost, you should be in a position to figure out your exact raise. If you collect a $2,095 monthly benefit, which is what the average retiree on Social Security receives, a 3.6% COLA adds $75 per month to your monthly checks. 
 Now, subtract $6.50 for the Medicare increase, and you're left with a net raise of $68.50 per month, or $822 per year. You can apply the same math to your specific benefit, but remember to factor in IRMAAs if they apply to you. 
 Of course, if you're worried about covering your costs given that your COLA is getting partially whittled down by an uptick in Part B premiums, there are steps you can take to stretch your Social Security benefits further. For one thing, you could try reducing spending in different categories to free up some funds. Working part-time could also help you better make ends meet in 2027. 
 Finally, choose your Medicare coverage carefully. Switching to a different Part D drug plan or Medicare Advantage plan for 2027 could lower your costs. Medicare's annual open enrollment period will remain in effect until Dec. 7, so you still have a bit of time to make changes to your coverage ahead of the new year.
